01 / LISTEN

Hear the universe.

Gravitational waves stretch and squeeze space. Shift their frequencies into our hearing range, and a merger sounds like a chirp.

02 / RECREATE

Be the black holes.

Hum, whistle, or say “whoooop” for 1.5 seconds after the countdown. Follow the curve: a gentle rise, then a faster sweep at the end.

03 / DISCOVER

Loud isn’t enough.

As noise increases, a convincing signal needs the right shape. Learn how consistency tests help separate chirps from glitches.

Inside the detector Educational model · how the scores work

A voice-sized analogy for a cosmic search

This is an outreach simulation, not a gravitational-wave analysis pipeline. The target is an accelerating 180–720 Hz sweep, not a physical binary waveform. Each attempt has a three-second countdown followed by a 1.5-second recording. The first countdown second measures background noise; stay quiet until the recording begins. The microphone turns off after each attempt. You can choose a lower or higher register below. Noise is added numerically to the captured audio, not played into the room.

Chirp match: compares the strongest spectral peak in each time frame with the rising target, allowing a small pitch tolerance. It is a time–frequency shape score, not matched-filter SNR.

chisquared: divides the expected chirp power into six equal-power time regions and compares each region’s measured, background-subtracted ridge energy with its expected share. The displayed χ²-like score uses a heuristic noise scale. Lower values mean a more consistent envelope; it is not the Allen frequency-bin χ² or a calibrated reduced χ².

chisquared_sgveto: projects the end of the recording onto short Gaussian-windowed sine/cosine tiles above the target’s final frequency, normalised by an earlier noise recording. Excess tile energy raises the score. This illustrates a sine-Gaussian veto; it is not PyCBC’s implementation or a statistically calibrated veto. Voice harmonics can also raise it: try a soft hum or whistle.

Real searches use noise-weighted matched filtering, frequency-bin χ² and sine-Gaussian checks. Read the PyCBC veto documentation ↗. Thresholds here are chosen for gameplay. A pass is a teaching outcome, not a detection claim.
